questions.text: Based on the specifications in "Translating PWD Rights", if a project requires 1200 mm, what is the correct interpretation?

options.text: 1200 mm is the minimum/standard requirement
1200 mm is the maximum permitted value
1200 mm applies only to specific conditions
1200 mm is an approximate value subject to interpretation

questions.rationale: The article specifies 1200 mm as the requirement. Context: 0–600 mm AFF** (low, reachable from floor). Do NOT confuse with light switches (...

questions.text: The mnemonic "FIRE" presented in "Translating PWD Rights" helps remember:

options.text: An outdated standard no longer in use
≤3 flashes/sec
A different concept from another subject area
A trap commonly tested on the ALE

questions.rationale: The mnemonic "FIRE" was specifically designed to help remember ≤3 flashes/sec.

questions.text: Under BP 344 Section 6, the emergency call button inside an accessible toilet cubicle must be mounted at which height above finished floor?

options.text: 400–600 mm AFF, so it remains reachable by a person who has fallen to the floor
900–1000 mm AFF, consistent with lever door handles and standard reach range
1100–1200 mm AFF, aligned with the Braille elevator panel mounting height
700–800 mm AFF, matching the grab bar height above the WC seat surface

rationale.summary: The call button must be reachable from the floor if the user has fallen.
rationale.explanation: BP 344 Sec. 6 specifies 400–600 mm AFF for the emergency call button — low enough to be reached by a person lying on the floor. This is a life-safety requirement, not a convenience dimension. At 900 mm or higher the button cannot be reached by a fallen occupant.
common_misconceptions: Confusing the call button height with lever handle height (900 mm AFF)
Confusing it with Braille panel height on elevator jambs (1200 mm AFF)

questions.explanation: 400–600 mm AFF is explicitly stated in BP 344 Sec. 6 so a fallen user can activate the alarm.

questions.text: A hospital pharmacy counter is designed with a single counter surface at 900 mm AFF and no knee clearance below. Which specific dimension must be added to make the counter accessible to a wheelchair user under BP 344 Sec. 14?

options.text: An adjustable counter spanning 750–950 mm AFF with 600 mm knee clearance
A pull-out shelf at 850 mm AFF with 500 mm knee clearance beneath it
A lower counter section at 750 mm AFF with 700 mm knee clearance beneath it
A lowered section at 800 mm AFF with 650 mm knee clearance beneath it

rationale.summary: BP 344 Sec. 14 requires a two-level counter: lower level at exactly 750 mm AFF with 700 mm knee clearance.
rationale.explanation: The two-level service counter standard sets the lower level at 750 mm AFF with 700 mm high × 480 mm deep knee clearance. This allows a wheelchair user to pull up to the counter and transact. An 800 mm or 850 mm surface is too high for comfortable wheelchair use and does not match the specified standard.
common_misconceptions: Assuming any lowered counter below 900 mm is compliant — the spec is precisely 750 mm
Confusing lavatory rim height (800 mm) with counter height (750 mm)

questions.explanation: The two-level counter requires a 750 mm lower level with 700 mm knee clearance per BP 344 Sec. 14.

questions.text: A 500-seat cinema is being designed. Under the 2024 IRR 3% rule, how many wheelchair spaces are required, and what is the clear floor dimension of each space?

options.text: 6 wheelchair spaces, each 800 mm wide × 1100 mm deep, based on the tiered table
15 wheelchair spaces, each 900 mm wide × 1200 mm deep, on a firm level surface
10 wheelchair spaces, each 900 mm wide × 1200 mm deep, based on 2% of capacity
15 wheelchair spaces, each 750 mm wide × 1000 mm deep, per the old IRR table

rationale.summary: 2024 IRR: 3% × 500 = 15 spaces; each space is 900 mm × 1200 mm.
rationale.explanation: The 2024 IRR replaced the old tiered table with a flat 3% rule. 3% of 500 = 15 spaces. Each wheelchair space must be 900 mm wide × 1200 mm deep, on a clear, firm, level surface, with access that does not pass through another wheelchair space. Option B reflects the outdated tiered table (301–500 seats = 6 spaces).
common_misconceptions: Applying the old tiered table (301–500 = 6 spaces) when the question specifies 2024 IRR
Using 2% instead of 3% for the wheelchair space count

questions.explanation: 3% × 500 = 15 spaces at 900 × 1200 mm each under the 2024 IRR flat-rate rule.

questions.text: The Right to Health (RA 7277 Sec. 23) requires accessible hospital toilets. What are the minimum clear internal dimensions of the accessible WC cubicle under BP 344 Sec. 6?

options.text: 2000 mm wide × 2000 mm deep, with a 900 mm door that slides only
1500 mm wide × 1800 mm deep, with a 750 mm door that swings inward
1800 mm wide × 1800 mm deep, with a 900 mm door that swings inward
1800 mm wide × 2250 mm deep, with a 900 mm door that swings out or slides

rationale.summary: Minimum accessible WC cubicle: 1800 mm × 2250 mm with 900 mm out-swinging or sliding door.
rationale.explanation: BP 344 Sec. 6 specifies a minimum 1800 mm × 2250 mm clear internal dimension for the accessible WC cubicle. The door must be 900 mm clear width and swing outward (or slide) so it does not block a wheelchair user who may have fallen against it. A 1500 mm or 1800 × 1800 mm cubicle is insufficient to contain the 1500 × 1500 mm turning space plus the WC fixtures.
common_misconceptions: Assuming 1800 × 1800 mm is sufficient — the 2250 mm depth is needed to fit turning space plus fixtures
Allowing an inward-swinging door — this would be blocked if the user falls against it

questions.explanation: 1800 × 2250 mm clear with a 900 mm out-swinging or sliding door is the BP 344 Sec. 6 minimum.

questions.text: A visual fire alarm strobe is specified for all hotel rooms under the Right to Information (RA 7277 Sec. 29) and BP 344 Sec. 17.8. What is the maximum flash rate and the minimum luminous intensity?

options.text: Maximum 3 flashes per second (3 Hz) and minimum 2 candelas; lens must be white
Minimum 3 flashes per second (3 Hz) and minimum 5 candelas; lens may be any color
Maximum 5 flashes per second (5 Hz) and minimum 2 candelas; lens must be white
Maximum 3 flashes per second (3 Hz) and minimum 10 candelas; lens must be red

rationale.summary: BP 344 Sec. 17.8: maximum 3 flashes/sec, minimum 2 candelas, white lens.
rationale.explanation: The flash rate ceiling of 3 Hz (not a minimum) exists because faster flashing can trigger seizures in photosensitive persons. The minimum intensity is 2 candelas and the lens must be white (not red or amber). The word 'FIRE' must also be visible on the unit. Option B incorrectly states 3 flashes/sec as a minimum — this is the most common exam trap.
common_misconceptions: Treating '3 flashes/sec' as a minimum instead of a maximum
Choosing a red lens — BP 344 specifies white

questions.explanation: Maximum 3 Hz, minimum 2 candelas, white lens per BP 344 Sec. 17.8 — flash rate is a ceiling, not a floor.

questions.text: An architect is designing a grab bar for the side wall of an accessible WC cubicle. The WC seat height is 460 mm AFF. At what height above finished floor should the horizontal grab bar be mounted?

options.text: 900 mm AFF — matching the lever handle and handrail height standard
300 mm AFF — as stated in the BP 344 grab bar specification
760 mm AFF — 300 mm above the 460 mm WC seat height
760 mm AFF — measured from the finished ceiling down to bar centerline

rationale.summary: Grab bar = 300 mm above WC seat AFF; with seat at 460 mm, bar is at 760 mm AFF.
rationale.explanation: BP 344 Sec. 6 states the grab bar is placed 300 mm above the WC seat height, not 300 mm above the floor. With a seat at 460 mm AFF, the bar is at 460 + 300 = 760 mm AFF. The most common trap is reading '300 mm' as the absolute AFF height rather than as the offset above the seat.
common_misconceptions: Reading '300 mm' as the bar's AFF height rather than the offset above the WC seat
Using 900 mm AFF, which is the handrail height, not the grab bar height

questions.explanation: Grab bar height = WC seat height + 300 mm per BP 344 Sec. 6; 460 + 300 = 760 mm AFF.

questions.text: A 4-storey school building claims compliance with RA 7277 Sec. 12 (Right to Education) by providing one accessible toilet on the ground floor only, arguing that the elevator serves all floors. Is this compliant under BP 344?

options.text: Yes — elevator access to the ground floor toilet satisfies the per-floor requirement
No — BP 344 requires at least one accessible toilet on each floor, regardless of elevator access
Yes — one accessible toilet per building is sufficient for schools under 5 storeys
No — but one accessible toilet per two floors is acceptable when an elevator is provided

rationale.summary: BP 344 requires one accessible toilet per floor — the elevator does not substitute for this requirement.
rationale.explanation: The elevator provides vertical access to each floor, but an accessible toilet must exist on each floor served by the building. A PWD should never have to travel to a different floor to use an accessible toilet. 'Per floor' means each floor — not one per building or one per two floors.
common_misconceptions: Believing that elevator access to a ground-floor toilet satisfies the per-floor requirement
Assuming 'per building' or 'per two floors' is acceptable under BP 344

questions.explanation: BP 344 mandates at least one accessible toilet per floor — the elevator argument does not satisfy this requirement.

questions.text: Under RA 7277 Sec. 30 (Right to Recreation), what height must the transfer wall at an accessible swimming pool be, and what transfer space must adjoin it?

options.text: Transfer wall at 480 mm AFF; adjoining transfer space 1500 × 1500 mm, slope ≤1:20
Transfer wall at 750 mm AFF; adjoining transfer space 1200 × 1200 mm, slope ≤1:20
Transfer wall at 450 mm AFF; adjoining transfer space 900 × 1200 mm, level surface
Transfer wall at 450 mm AFF; adjoining transfer space 1500 × 1500 mm, slope ≤1:12

rationale.summary: Pool transfer wall = 450 mm AFF; transfer space = 1500 × 1500 mm with approach slope ≤1:12.
rationale.explanation: BP 344 Sec. 1 specifies the pool transfer wall at 450 mm AFF — a height that allows a wheelchair user to slide laterally from chair to pool edge. The 1500 × 1500 mm transfer space beside the wall must have an approach slope of ≤1:12. The 450 mm figure is specific to pool transfer walls only; do not confuse it with WC seat height (450–480 mm) which is a coincidental overlap.
common_misconceptions: Confusing the transfer wall height (450 mm) with WC seat height or grab bar offset
Using 750 mm, which is the lower service counter height, not the pool transfer wall

questions.explanation: Pool transfer wall = 450 mm AFF; transfer space = 1500 × 1500 mm per BP 344 Sec. 1.

questions.text: An accessible workstation in an office building (Right to Employment, RA 7277 Sec. 5–8) must meet which set of dimensions under BP 344 Sec. 15?

options.text: Width ≥900 mm; knee clearance 700 mm high × 480 mm deep; 1500 × 1500 mm turning space beside the workstation
Width ≥750 mm; knee clearance 650 mm high × 500 mm deep; 1200 × 1200 mm turning space beside the workstation
Width ≥900 mm; knee clearance 750 mm high × 480 mm deep; 1800 × 1800 mm turning space beside the workstation
Width ≥1200 mm; knee clearance 700 mm high × 600 mm deep; 1500 × 1500 mm turning space at the end of the row

rationale.summary: Accessible workstation: width ≥900 mm, knee clearance 700 mm × 480 mm, turning space 1500 × 1500 mm beside it.
rationale.explanation: BP 344 Sec. 15 specifies the accessible workstation width at a minimum of 900 mm, knee clearance of 700 mm high × 480 mm deep, and a 1500 × 1500 mm turning space beside (not at the end of the row). The 750 mm height appears in counter and table contexts; the 700 mm figure is specifically for knee clearance under workstations.
common_misconceptions: Using 650 mm or 750 mm knee clearance — the workstation standard is 700 mm
Placing the turning space at the row end rather than beside the specific accessible station

questions.explanation: Accessible workstation per BP 344 Sec. 15: 900 mm wide, 700 × 480 mm knee clearance, 1500 × 1500 mm turning space alongside.

questions.text: A senior architect reviews a transit terminal design and finds the accessible parking stalls are 3500 mm wide with a 1500 mm shared aisle, located at the far end of the lot. Which two non-compliances must be corrected under BP 344?

options.text: Stall width must be 3700 mm and the access aisle 1200 mm; stalls must be nearest the accessible entrance
Stall width must be 4000 mm and the access aisle 1800 mm; stalls must be nearest the accessible entrance
Stall width must be 4000 mm and the access aisle 1800 mm; vertical clearance must be 2300 mm
Stall width must be 5000 mm and the access aisle 1800 mm; stalls must be nearest the accessible entrance

rationale.summary: Accessible parking stall = 4000 mm wide; access aisle = 1800 mm; location = nearest accessible entrance.
rationale.explanation: BP 344 requires accessible parking stalls to be 4000 mm wide × 5000 mm long with a 1800 mm access aisle (for ramp deployment and side transfer). The stalls must be on the shortest accessible route to the accessible entrance — placing them at the far end of the lot is a location non-compliance. Option B confuses the hospital/mall checklist stall with a narrower value; 3700 mm appears in some typology table variants but 4000 mm is the standard accessible stall width.
common_misconceptions: Using 3700 mm stall width from some checklist variants instead of the standard 4000 mm
Focusing only on dimension errors and missing the location requirement

questions.explanation: Stall width 4000 mm, access aisle 1800 mm, and nearest-to-entrance location are all mandatory per BP 344.
